So this is where it happens. I have to admit, I came expecting finished pieces, and there is nothing on the walls.
There is nothing on the walls. What you are looking at is the research. This is practice-based research, and the making and the thinking are one act.
Then help me. What is the premise?
That illness produces a kind of knowledge medicine has no room for. I have been testing that idea since 2015.
Ten years on one idea. What has changed in that time?
The premise has not changed. The strands have. I started with photographs, and for the last three years I have been working almost entirely with the field notes and the recorded voices.
And the outcome? I ask because a board will ask me.
The outcome is that somebody else can enter the question now. That is a tentative answer, and I would rather give you a tentative one than a tidy one.
The research is the work, not the preparation for it.

The outcome is not an object, and I am comfortable saying that.

People often ask me when the work will be finished, and I have stopped apologizing for the answer. I have been working on the same question since 2015, and the question has not run out yet. What I make along the way, the notebooks, the recordings, the conversations I have with people who have been ill for a long time, those are not preparation for the work. They are the work. I think the hardest part of explaining practice-based research is that it has no single object at the end of it. There is no canvas you can point at. What there is, if I am honest, is a body of work that keeps changing shape, and a premise I have tested so many times that I now trust it. Somebody asked me last year what my outcome was. I said the outcome is that I understand the question better than I did ten years ago, and that other people can now enter it. She looked disappointed. I have made my peace with that.

I do maybe forty studio visits a year, and I can usually tell in the first ten minutes whether I am going to come back. It has almost nothing to do with how finished the work looks. What I am listening for is whether the artist can tell me what the work is asking. Not what it is about. What it is asking. If somebody gives me the premise in one sentence and then shows me three things that test it in completely different ways, I am interested, even if none of the three is resolved. The visits that go badly are the ones where the artist describes materials for forty minutes. I know what plaster is. What I do not know is why this person has been circling the same problem for eight years, and that is the only thing I came to find out. My advice, honestly, is to prepare two sentences and then stop talking and let me ask.

Welcome to the audio edition. This issue began with a complaint we kept hearing from artists who work with researchers, and from researchers who work with artists. Neither side believes the other one is producing knowledge. The scientists tend to think of the artwork as illustration, something that arrives at the end to make the findings easier to look at. The artists say the opposite, that the research is not raw material for a picture, it is the practice itself, and it unfolds on its own terms. In the six essays in this issue you will hear both positions defended by people who have spent decades on either side of the argument, and, in two cases, by people who have crossed over and now refuse to say which one they are. As always, the full text is on the site, and every essay is read aloud, so you can listen while you walk. We would rather you took your time with these. They are not short.
